(p-112) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah At-Tawbah

Know first that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did not write the line *Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim* (the basmalah, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") at the beginning of the surah called *Bara'ah* in the 'Uthmanic codices (al-masahif al-'Uthmaniyyah). The scholars differed on the reason the basmalah was omitted from it, and they gave several opinions:

Among them: the basmalah is mercy and security (aman), and *Bara'ah* was revealed with the sword, so there is no security in it. This opinion is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah.

Among them: this follows the custom of the Arabs, who, when they wrote a document that contained the breaking of a covenant, dropped the basmalah from it. When the Prophet ﷺ sent 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, to recite it to them at the season (al-mawsim), he recited it without saying the basmalah, following the Arab custom regarding the breaking of a covenant. Some scholars related this opinion, and its weakness is not hidden.

Among them: when the Companions disagreed over whether *Bara'ah* and *al-Anfal* were one surah or two, they left a gap between them for the view of those who said they were two surahs, and they omitted the basmalah for the view of those who said they were one surah. Both parties were satisfied, and the proof of each was preserved in the codex.

Among them: the first part of the surah *Bara'ah* was abrogated (nusikha, naskh), and the basmalah fell away with it. This opinion was narrated by Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qasim, and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, from Malik, as al-Qurtubi reported.

It is also related from Ibn 'Ajlan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it was equal to Surah *al-Baqarah* in length.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The correct view is that the basmalah was not written in this surah, because Jibril did not bring it down with it." This was said by al-Qushayri. End of quotation.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The most apparent of the opinions to me on this question is that the reason for the omission of the basmalah in this surah is what 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Ibn 'Abbas.

An-Nasa'i, at-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Imam Ahmad, and Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih*, and al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak*, who said: "Its isnad is sahih, though they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not include it," reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I said to 'Uthman: "What led you to put *al-Anfal*, which is among the *mathani* (the shorter oft-repeated surahs), and *Bara'ah*, which is among the *mi'in* (the surahs of about a hundred verses), together, and you did not write the line *Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim* [al-Fatihah: 1] between them, and you placed them among the *as-sab' at-tiwal* (the seven long surahs)? What led you to do that?"

'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when something was revealed to him, would call some of those who wrote for him and say: 'Place this in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned.' And verses would be revealed to him and he would say: 'Place these verses in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned.' *Al-Anfal* was among the first things revealed at Medina, and *Bara'ah* was among the last things revealed of the Qur'an. Its story resembled its story, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away without explaining to us that it was part of it. So I thought it was part of it. For this reason I put the two together, and I did not write the line *Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim* [al-Fatihah: 1] between them, and I placed it among the seven long surahs." End of quotation.

Two notes

The first: From this hadith it is understood that the arrangement of the verses of the Qur'an was by divine direction (tawqif) from the Prophet ﷺ, and this is so beyond doubt. It is also understood from it that the arrangement of its surahs was by tawqif as well, apart from Surah *Bara'ah*. This is the most apparent of the opinions, and the hadith's indication of it is clear.

The second note: Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "In this hadith is evidence that qiyas (analogical reasoning) is a foundation of the religion. Do you not see how 'Uthman and the eminent Companions resorted to analogy by resemblance (qiyas ash-shabah) when there was no explicit text, and they saw that the story of *Bara'ah* resembled the story of *al-Anfal*, so they attached it to it? If qiyas enters into the compilation of the Qur'an, then what do you think about the rest of the rulings?"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger toward those with whom you made covenants﴾, up to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿four months﴾.

The apparent meaning of this noble verse is general, covering all covenanted disbelievers, and that after the expiry of the four months of respite mentioned in His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ [at-Tawbah: 2], there is no covenant for any disbeliever.

On this there is much disagreement among the scholars. What the Qur'an clarifies, and what is supported by some of those opinions, is that this applies only to those with unrestricted covenants that are not limited to a specific time, or to those whose fixed-term covenant has less than four months remaining, so that they are given four months in full. As for those whose fixed-term covenant has more than four months remaining, it is obligatory to complete their term. The Qur'anic evidence that explains this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, then they have not failed you in anything nor supported anyone against you; so fulfill their covenant to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ [at-Tawbah: 4]. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir, and it is related from al-Kalbi, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and others. Ibn Kathir said this. It is supported by the hadith of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ sent him with four matters when *Bara'ah* was revealed: "No naked person is to circumambulate the House; no polytheist is to approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs; whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it extends to its term; and no one enters Paradise except a believing soul."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 9, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾.

Some scholars said: The start of the respite (ta'jil) for the four months mentioned was from Shawwal, and its end was the close of Muharram. This was also the view of al-Zuhri, may Allah have mercy on him. However, the Qur'an indicates that its beginning was from the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), according to the more correct view that it is the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage (yawm al-hajj al-akbar), or the Day of 'Arafah according to the view that it is the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage﴾. This is explicit that the beginning of the aforementioned announcement was from the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage, which is the Day of Sacrifice. It is not hidden that its end was at the tenth of Rabi' al-Thani.

Ibn Kathir said, in his commentary on this verse: "al-Zuhri said: The start of the respite was from Shawwal, and its end was the close of Muharram. This view is strange. How could they be held accountable for a period whose ruling had not reached them? Their matter only became manifest to them on the Day of Sacrifice, when the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proclaimed it. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage﴾."

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Except those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists, then they have not failed you in anything, nor have they supported anyone against you, so fulfill their treaty to them until their term.﴾

It is understood from the implication of the opposite (mafhum al-mukhalafa, the argument by contrary implication) of this verse that if the polytheists break the covenant, it is permissible to fight them. A similar example is the Exalted's saying: ﴿So as long as they are upright with you, be upright with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 7]. This implication in the two verses is stated explicitly by the Exalted in His saying: ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief—indeed, they have no oaths—so that they may cease﴾ [al-Tawbah: 12].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 9, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed⁠—﴾ the verse.

The scholars differed concerning what is meant by "the sacred months" in this verse.

Ibn Jarir said: they are the ones mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Of them, four are sacred. That is the upright religion, so do not wrong yourselves within them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], as Abu Ja'far al-Baqir said.

But Ibn Jarir also said: the last of the sacred months, in their case, is Muharram. Something similar to this view was related by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak adopted it.

However, the context indicates that what is meant by them is the months of respite mentioned in His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾.

Ibn Kathir said, in his commentary on this verse: "What appears from the context is what Ibn Abbas held, in the narration of al-Awfi from him, and this was also the view of Mujahid, Amr ibn Shu'ayb, Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam: that what is meant by them is the four months explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾. Then He said: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], meaning: when the four months have ended, which We made sacred for you to fight them in, and granted them respite in, then wherever you find them, kill them. This is because returning the reference to something already mentioned is better than to something merely implied, and because the sacred four months will have their ruling explained in another verse." End of quote.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-297) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾.

Know first that what is meant by these sacred months is the months of grace stated in His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ [9], not the sacred months which are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab according to the correct view. This is the view of Ibn Abbas in al-Awfi's narration from him.

Mujahid, Amr ibn Shu'ayb, Muhammad ibn Ishaq, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam also held this view. Ibn Kathir preferred this opinion because the context of the Qur'an points to it, and it differs from the views of Ibn Jarir.

Accordingly, the verse by its generality indicates fighting the disbelievers in the well-known sacred months after the four months of respite have ended. Another verse indicates that fighting is not to be done in them: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred. That is the upright religion, so do not wrong yourselves within them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

The answer is that the prohibition of the sacred months has been abrogated (mansukh) by the generality of the verses of the sword. Whoever says there is no abrogation says that it specifies (takhsis) them. The apparent correct view is that they are abrogated, as is indicated by the action of the Prophet (ﷺ) in besieging Thaqif during the sacred month, which is Dhu al-Qa'dah. It is established in the two Sahihs that he went out against Hawazin in Shawwal; when he defeated them, seized their property, and their scattered forces returned, they took refuge in al-Ta'if. He then went to al-Ta'if and besieged them for forty days, then withdrew without conquering it. Thus it is established that he besieged during a sacred month. This view is the well-known one among the scholars. Accordingly, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ abrogates His saying ﴿Of them, four are sacred﴾,

• and His saying: ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month﴾ [5],

• and His saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 194].

(p-298)

What is abrogated from these, and from His saying ﴿four are sacred﴾, is the prohibition of the month in the first and of the months in the second only, not what they contain of information, because information cannot be abrogated in law.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 9, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they planned to expel the Messenger﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted mentions that the disbelievers of Makkah planned to expel him ﷺ from Makkah. In other places He states explicitly that they actually expelled him, such as:

• His saying: ﴿They expel the Messenger and yourselves﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and the verse continues;

• and His saying: ﴿And how many a city, mightier in strength than your city which has expelled you﴾ [Muhammad: 13];

• and His saying: ﴿If you do not support him, Allah has already supported him when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], and the verse continues. He also mentions in other places their attempts to expel him before they actually did so, such as:

• His saying: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you, or kill you, or expel you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30],

and His saying: ﴿And indeed, they almost unsettled you from the land to expel you from it﴾.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 9, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith﴾ — the verse.

In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted forbids taking the disbelievers as allies (muwalah), even if they are close relatives. In another place He stated that adherence to the attribute of faith prevents affection (muwaddah) toward the disbelievers, even if they are close relatives. This is His saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kinsmen﴾ — the verse [al-Mujadila: 22].

He, the Exalted, mentioned what befell the Muslims on the day of Hunayn in this noble verse. He mentioned what befell them on the day of Uhud with His words: ﴿When you were climbing up, not turning aside for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 153]. He stated explicitly that He had turned in forgiveness toward those who turned away on the day of Uhud with His words: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. And Allah has already pardoned them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 155]. Here He indicated His turning in forgiveness toward those who turned away on the day of Hunayn with His words: ﴿Then Allah will turn in forgiveness after that to whom He wills. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 26], as some scholars have also indicated.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 9, verse 30:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah."﴾ - to His saying - ﴿Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him.﴾

This verse contains explicit clear statement that the disbelievers among the People of the Book are polytheists (mushrikun), by the evidence of His saying about them: ﴿Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him﴾, after He had explained the aspects of their polytheism, by their attributing offspring to Allah and their taking the rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa: 48], since the scholars are in consensus (ijma') that the disbelieving People of the Book are included in it.

Other verses have come which apparently indicate that the People of the Book are not among the polytheists, such as:

- His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to be separated﴾ - the verse [98],
- and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell﴾ - the verse [al-Bayyinah: 6],
- and His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, wish that there be sent down to you﴾ - the verse [al-Baqarah: 105].

And conjunction (al-'atf) requires difference (al-mughayarah).

What appears to me, its compiler, may Allah pardon him, is that the way of reconciling is that major shirk (al-shirk al-akbar), which necessitates exit from the religion (al-milla), has types. The People of the Book are characterized by some of them and not characterized by another type of them. As for the type which they are not characterized by, it is what the disbelievers of Makkah were characterized by, namely the explicit worship of idols. For this reason He joined them to them, because the disbelievers of Makkah were characterized by the worship of idols, which the People of the Book were not characterized by. This difference is what justified the conjunction. So it does not negate that the People of the Book are polytheists by another type of major shirk, which is obedience to Satan and to the rabbis and monks. For the one who obeys Satan, if he believes that this is correct, is then a worshipper of Satan, a polytheist by worship of Satan with the major shirk that makes one abide eternally in the Fire, as the Qur'anic texts have made clear, such as His saying: ﴿They invoke besides Him none but females, and they invoke none but a rebellious Satan﴾ [al-Nisa: 117]. So His saying ﴿and they invoke none but a Satan﴾ ... is valid ... its meaning is: and they do not worship except Satan, because their worship of Satan is their obedience to him in what Allah has forbidden for them. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan?﴾ - the verse [Ya-Sin: 60].

And His saying, exalted is He, about His close friend Ibrahim: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has ever been to the Most Merciful a disobedient one﴾ (p-299) [Maryam: 44], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ - the verse [Saba': 41].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus their partners have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ - the verse [al-An'am: 137]. So all this disbelief is by the shirk of obedience in disobedience to Allah, exalted is He. "When Satan inspired the disbelievers of Makkah to ask the Prophet ﷺ about the sheep that dies, who killed it; and that if he ﷺ said, 'Allah killed it,' they would say: 'What we have killed with our hands is lawful, and what Allah has killed is unlawful, so you are then better than Allah,' Allah revealed in that His saying: ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you; and if you obey them, indeed you are then polytheists﴾" [al-An'am: 121]. So He, exalted, swore in this verse that whoever obeys Satan in disobedience to Allah is a polytheist with Allah. And when "'Adi ibn Hatim asked the Prophet ﷺ about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They took their rabbis and monks as lords﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31], how did they take them as lords? The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Did they not make lawful for them what Allah had forbidden, and make unlawful for them what Allah had made lawful, and they followed them?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'By that they took them as lords.'" Thus it becomes clear that the People of the Book are polytheists in this respect with the major shirk, even if the disbelievers of Makkah were in the explicit worship of idols. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾. The most evident of the opinions, and the closest to correctness, regarding the meaning of ﴿hoard﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34] in this noble verse, is that what is meant by their hoarding gold and silver, and by their not spending them in the way of Allah, is that they do not pay their zakah (obligatory alms) on them.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (exegesis) of this verse: "As for al-kanz (hoarding), Malik narrated from Abdullah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar: it is the wealth whose zakah is not paid."

Al-Thawri and others narrated from Ubaydullah, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: "Whatever its zakah has been paid is not hoarding, even if it is beneath seven earths; and whatever is apparent and whose zakah is not paid is hoarding." This has also been related from Ibn Abbas, Jabir and Abu Hurayrah, both as a statement of their own (mawquf) and as a prophetic report (marfu').

Umar ibn al-Khattab said something similar: "Any wealth whose zakah has been paid is not hoarding, even if it is buried in the earth; and any wealth whose zakah has not been paid is hoarding, by which its owner will be branded, even if it is on the surface of the earth." End of quotation.

Among those from whom this opinion has been related are Ikrimah and al-Suddi. There is no doubt that this opinion is the most correct of the opinions, because whoever pays the obligatory right in wealth, which is zakah, will not be branded with what remains if he withholds it, since zakah purifies it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. Moreover, inheritance was only prescribed for wealth that remains after its owners.

Among the clearest proofs in this regard is the hadith of Talhah ibn Ubaydullah and others, concerning the story of the Bedouin, brother of the Banu Sa'd from Hawazin, who is Dimam ibn Tha'labah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed him that Allah had made zakah obligatory upon him. He said: "Is there anything else obligatory upon me besides it?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "No, unless you choose to give voluntarily."

Also the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. We have already established in al-Baqarah, with verification, that it refers to what exceeds the need that cannot be dispensed with. Also his saying (ﷺ): "There is no charity due on less than five wasq," the hadith; because ṣadaqah is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it generalises the negation of every charity.

There are other opinions regarding the verse:

Among them: that it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verses of zakah, such as the statement: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity, by which you purify them﴾, the verse.

Al-Bukhari also related this opinion of abrogation from Ibn Umar, and Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz and Iraq ibn Malik also held it. End of quotation.

And from Ali that he said: "Four thousand (dirhams) or less is an expenditure, and whatever is more than that is hoarding." The position of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding this verse is well known: that it is forbidden for a person to save anything beyond the maintenance of his dependants. End of quotation. It is not hidden that saving what has had its obligatory rights paid is not objectionable, and it is like a necessity according to the general body of Muslims.

If it is said: what is the answer to what Imam Ahmad narrated, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A man from the People of the Suffah died and left two dinars or two dirhams, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Two brands, pray over your companion.'" End of quotation. And what Qatadah narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Umamah Sudayy ibn Ajlan, who said: "A man from the People of the Suffah died, and a dinar was found in his loincloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A brand.' Then another died, and two dinars were found in his loincloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Two brands.'" And what Abd al-Razzaq and others narrated, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver," saying it three times. This was grievous to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: "Then what wealth should we acquire?" Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I will learn it for you from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So he said: "O Messenger of Allah, your companions have been distressed, and they say: 'Then what wealth should we acquire?'" He said: "A tongue that remembers, a heart that is grateful, and a wife who helps one of you in his religion." And similar to that from the hadiths.

The answer, and Allah knows best, is that this severity was at first, then it was abrogated by the prescription of zakah, as al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Many reports have come from Abu Dharr indicating that he held that every accumulated wealth that exceeds sustenance and a sufficient livelihood is hoarding, whose doer is blameworthy, and that the verse of warning was revealed concerning that. The majority of the Companions and those after them disagreed with him, and they applied the warning to the withholder of zakah, until (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: "This was obligatory at the beginning, then it was abrogated." Then he mentioned from Shaddad ibn Aws that he said: "Abu Dharr used to hear a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) containing severity, then he would go out to his people and then the Prophet (ﷺ) would grant a concession regarding it, but he would not hear the concession, and would hold to the first command." End of quotation.

Some scholars said: it is specific to the People of the Book, based on its being joined with the statement: ﴿Indeed, many of the rabbis and monks﴾, the verse [al-Tawbah: 34].

Since you know that the verified position is that the verse is general, and that it concerns the one who does not pay zakah, then know that what is meant by it is what is referred to in the verses of zakah. We have already mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that when the explanation by the Qur'an is not sufficient for the intended meaning, we complete the explanation from the Sunnah, insofar as it is an explanation of the Qur'an that is being explained by it. And the verses of zakah,

• such as the statement: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾, the verse,
• and the statement: ﴿And give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43],
• and the statement: ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267],

do not suffice for the explanation, so it is explained by the Sunnah. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad the Malikite said: this verse includes the zakah on property in its specific form (zakat al-ayn), which is obligatory under four conditions: freedom, Islam, the passing of a full year (hawl), and a nisab (threshold) free of debt. End of quotation. Some of these conditions are subject to disagreement.

Issues arising from the rulings of this noble verse

The first issue: concerning the nisab of gold and silver, and the amount due to be paid from them.

As for the nisab of silver, all the scholars have agreed that it is two hundred dirhams of the legal weight. The weight of the legal dirham is six daniq, and every ten legal dirhams equal seven mithqals, and the uqiyyah is forty legal dirhams.

All of this is agreed upon by the Muslims, so no account is taken of the view of al-Marisi, who broke the consensus by it, which is to consider the number of dirhams rather than their weight; nor of what al-Sarakhsi of the Shafi'is uniquely held, claiming it was a view within the school, that a debased dirham, if its value were added to the value of the alloy, such as copper for example, would reach the nisab, that zakah is due on it, as was related from Abu Hanifah; nor of the view of Ibn Habib al-Andalusi, that the people of each land deal with their own dirhams; nor of what Ibn Abd al-Barr mentioned regarding the difference in weight between the dirhams of al-Andalus and other city dirhams; because the clear sound texts, on which the Muslims agree, make clear that the nisab of silver is two hundred legal dirhams by the weight that was known in Makkah. End of quotation.

[Continuing to p. 435:] And every seven mithqals are ten dirhams. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related in their two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no charity due on less than five uqiyyah." Muslim related it in his Sahih from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him. All the Muslims and the majority of the people of the Arabic language have agreed that the uqiyyah is forty dirhams. As for what Abu Ubayd and others mentioned, that the dirham's measure was unknown until Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan came, gathered the scholars, and they made every ten dirhams equal seven mithqals, its falsity is not hidden; and it is not possible that the nisab of zakah and the amputation threshold for theft were unknown in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his rightly-guided successors, may Allah be pleased with them, until Abd al-Malik verified it. The apparent meaning of what was transmitted in this regard is that none of them were minted by Islam, and they varied in weight relative to their number: ten, for example, might weigh ten, and ten might weigh eight; so opinion agreed that they should be inscribed with Arabic writing and made into one standard weight.

We have already mentioned the verification of the weight of the dirham in al-An'am. Some scholars said: a small deficiency is excused in the nisab of silver, a deficiency with which the dirhams still circulate as complete ones do.

The apparent meaning of the texts is that there is no zakah except on a complete nisab, because a deficient amount, even by a little, is truly less than five uqiyyah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) clearly stated that what is less than it has no charity due on it.

Once you have verified the text and the consensus, that the nisab of silver is two hundred legal dirhams, which is the weight of one hundred and forty mithqals of pure silver, know that the amount due from it is one-fortieth (rub' al-'ushr) by the consensus of the Muslims. It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "And in silver (al-riqqah) is one-fortieth," and al-riqqah is silver.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih, in the chapter "Zakah of Sheep": Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Muthanna al-Ansari narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: Thumamah ibn Abdullah ibn Anas narrated to me, that Anas narrated to him, that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote this letter for him when he sent him to Bahrain: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. This is the obligatory charity which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) enjoined upon the Muslims, and which Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ)..." the hadith. In it: "And for silver: one-fortieth," and this is a clear, sound text upon which all the Muslims agree.

It is thus established that there is no disagreement among the Muslims regarding the obligation of zakah on silver, no disagreement among them that its nisab is two hundred legal dirhams, and no disagreement among them that what is due on it is one-fortieth.

The majority of scholars hold that there is no waqs (fractional remainder) in it, contrary to Abu Hanifah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Sha'bi, Makhul, Amr ibn Dinar and al-Zuhri, who said: there is nothing in the excess over two hundred until it reaches forty, and then one dirham is due on it.

As for gold: the majority of the scholars of the Muslims hold that its nisab is twenty dinars, and the dinar is the mithqal. No account is taken of the one who deviated and opposed the majority of the scholars of the Muslims, such as what was related from al-Hasan in one of his two opinions: that the nisab of gold is forty dinars; and like the view of Tawus, that the nisab of gold is measured by its valuation in silver, so whatever reaches a value of two hundred dirhams, zakah is due on it. The majority of the scholars of the Muslims also hold that the amount due on it is one-fortieth.

The evidence for what we have mentioned from the majority of the scholars of the Ummah, that the nisab of gold is twenty dinars and the amount due on it is one-fortieth, is what Abu Dawud related in his Sunan: Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Mahri narrated to us, Ibn Wahb informed us, Jarir ibn Hazim informed me, and another man was named, from Abu Ishaq, from Asim ibn Damrah and al-Harith al-A'war, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you have two hundred dirhams and a year passes over them, then five dirhams are due on them, and nothing is due from you (meaning in gold) until you have twenty dinars. When you have twenty dinars and a year passes over them, then half a dinar is due on them, and whatever is more, then it is according to that proportion." He said: "I do not know whether Ali says 'and whatever is more, then it is according to that proportion,' or whether he raised it to the Prophet (ﷺ)? And there is no zakah on wealth until a year passes over it, except that Jarir said, Ibn Wahb adds in the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): 'There is no zakah on wealth until a year passes over it.'" End of quotation.

**The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 9, Verse 34 (Part 2 of 7)**

(p-121) If it is said: this hadith is weak, because of al-Harith al-A'war and Asim ibn Damra, since both of them are weak. Also, al-Daraqutni said: the correct version is that it is halted (mawquf) at Ali. Also, Ibn al-Mawwaq said: there is a hidden defect (illah khafiyya) in it, namely that Jarir ibn Hazim did not hear it from Abu Ishaq. The memorizers among the companions of Ibn Wahb, namely Sahnun, Harmala, Yunus, Bahr ibn Nasr and others, related it from Ibn Wahb, from Jarir ibn Hazim, and al-Harith ibn Nabhan, from al-Hasan ibn Umara, from Abu Ishaq, and he mentioned it. Ibn al-Mawwaq said: the blame for it falls on Sulayman, the teacher of Abu Dawud, for he erred in omitting (p-121) a man. End of quote. Also, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made the zakat on silver obligatory, and the Muslims after him took zakat on gold, either on the basis of a report from him that has not reached us, or by analogy. End of quote. This is explicit from al-Shafi'i that he holds that nothing is established concerning gold in his knowledge. Also, Ibn Abd al-Barr said: nothing has been established from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the zakat on gold through the transmission of trustworthy single narrators (ahad).

However, al-Hasan ibn Umara narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from Asim and al-Harith, from Ali, and he mentioned it. Abu Hanifa also narrated it likewise. Even if it were authentically from him, there would be no proof in it, because al-Hasan ibn Umara is abandoned (matruk).

Also, Ibn Hazm said: nothing has been established from the Prophet ﷺ concerning the nisab (threshold) of gold, nor concerning the obligatory amount due from it.

He also mentioned that the aforementioned hadith, in the narration of al-Harith al-A'war, is marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ), and al-Harith is weak and not to be used as proof, and more than one scholar has called him a liar. He said: as for the narration of Asim ibn Damra, it is mawquf (halted) at Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: likewise Shu'ba, Sufyan and Ma'mar narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from Asim, as mawquf. Every trustworthy narrator who related from Asim did likewise.

The answer comes in several aspects:

The first: some scholars said that this hadith is established. Al-Tirmidhi said: he narrated part of this hadith. This hadith was narrated by al-A'mash, Abu Awana and others, from Abu Ishaq, from Asim ibn Damra, from Ali. Sufyan al-Thawri, Ibn Uyayna and more than one other narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from al-Harith, from Ali. I asked Muhammad (i.e., al-Bukhari) about this hadith, and he said: both of them are sound (sahih) in my view. End of quote.

So you see that al-Tirmidhi transmitted from al-Bukhari the authentication (tashih) of this hadith. Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: as for the hadith of Asim from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, Abu Dawud and others narrated it with a fair (hasan) or sound (sahih) chain, from Ali, from the Prophet ﷺ. End of quote.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: the hadith of Ali is from the hadith of Abu Ishaq, from al-Harith al-A'war and Asim ibn Damra. It has already been mentioned that al-Bukhari said: both are sound in his view, and al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) has graded it as fair. End of quote; the point of al-Shawkani's words is here.

(p-122) The second aspect: it is strengthened by what al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Jahsh, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he commanded Mu'adh, when he sent him to Yemen, to take one dinar from every forty dinars. The hadith was mentioned by Ibn Hajar in al-Talkhis, and he remained silent about it. It is also strengthened by what Amr ibn Shu'ayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Nothing is due on less than twenty mithqals of gold." Al-Nawawi said: it is gharib (singular in its chain). End of quote.

The third aspect: a discussion according to the discipline of the science of hadith and the principles of jurisprudence. We say:

We grant that al-Harith al-A'war is weak, as was previously mentioned in Surah al-Ma'ida, even though Ibn Ma'in deemed him trustworthy. There remains Asim ibn Damra, with whom he narrated the hadith, and his narration is a proof. Ibn al-Madini deemed him trustworthy.

Al-Nasa'i said: there is nothing wrong with him.

Ibn Hajar said about him in al-Taqrib: Asim ibn Damra al-Salluli al-Kufi is truthful (saduq), and his narration is strengthened by the narration of al-Harith, even though al-Harith is weak. And [it is strengthened] by what we have mentioned from Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Jahsh and Amr ibn Shu'ayb.

From this you know that discrediting the hadith on account of the weakness of its chain is rejected.

We have already cited from al-Tirmidhi that al-Bukhari said: both are sound.

We have also already noted that al-Nawawi said of it: fair or sound.

Al-Shawkani transmitted from Ibn Hajar that he graded it as fair.

As for what Ibn al-Mawwaq used to criticize it, namely that Jarir ibn Hazim did not hear it from Abu Ishaq, because between them is al-Hasan ibn Umara, who is abandoned, this is rejected, because the hadith is established from multiple sound routes to Abu Ishaq. We have already noted that al-Tirmidhi said, and mentioned part of it: this hadith was narrated by al-A'mash, Abu Awana and others, from Abu Ishaq, from Asim ibn Damra, from Ali; and Sufyan al-Thawri, Ibn Uyayna and more than one other narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from al-Harith, from Ali. End of quote.

So you see that Abu Awana, al-A'mash, the two Sufyans and others all narrated it from Abu Ishaq.

Through this you know that Ibn al-Mawwaq's criticism, that its narrator from Abu Ishaq is al-Hasan ibn Umara, who is abandoned, is a baseless criticism, because the hadith is sound up to Abu Ishaq. When you have verified the rejection of its weakening on the ground that Asim is truthful, and the rejection of Ibn al-Mawwaq's criticism of it, know that Ibn Hazm's criticism of it, namely that the marfu' version is the narration of al-Harith, who is weak, and that the narration of Asim ibn Damra is mawquf at Ali, is rejected on two grounds:

The first: the amount of the zakat threshold and the amount due from it are both matters determined by revelation (tawqifi), with no room for opinion and personal reasoning (ijtihad). A mawquf report that is of this kind has the ruling of being traced to the Prophet ﷺ, as is known in the science of hadith and the principles of jurisprudence.

Al-Alawi al-Shinqiti said in Tal'at al-Anwar:

"What comes from a companion concerning a matter where opinion has no place according to them is considered marfu' (traced to the Prophet)."

Al-Iraqi said in his Alfiyya: [Rajaz meter]

"What comes from a companion in a way that cannot be called opinion, its ruling is raf' (attribution to the Prophet), as he said in al-Mahsul, like the one who comes... so the judge is to take it as raf' for this, and it is established."

The second: the chain of Abu Dawud through which he narrated it is fair or sound, as al-Nawawi and others said, and raf' (attribution) is an addition by trustworthy narrators, which is accepted. In Maraqi al-Su'ud:

"Raf', wasl (connection) and an increase in wording are accepted according to the imam of memorization..." etc.

The fourth aspect: the aforementioned hadith is reinforced by the ijma' (scholarly consensus) of the qualified scholars of the Muslims, except for one who departed from the majority (al-sawad al-a'zam) in acting according to its requirement. When the consensus of the Muslims agrees with a single report (khabar ahad), some scholars say: by the consensus agreeing with it, it becomes definitive (qat'i) like the mutawatir (widely transmitted report).

Most of the usul scholars say: it does not become definitive by that.

Some made a distinction, saying: if they explicitly state that their reliance in their consensus is that report, it conveys certainty; otherwise it does not. Al-Marāqī al-Su'ud alludes to this in his words: [Rajaz meter]

"What agrees with the consensus does not convey certainty, and some speak of certainty; and some hold it conveys it when they rely upon it..." etc.

In any case, it is not hidden that it is strengthened by the practice of the Muslims according to it.

The fifth: the evidence of the Book and the consensus that zakat is obligatory on gold.

As for the Book, it is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah, give them tidings of a painful punishment, on the Day when they will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with them: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard."﴾ [al-Tawba: 34–35].

As for the Sunnah: it is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No owner of gold or silver does not pay its due from them, except that on the Day of Resurrection plates of fire will be made for him, and they will be heated in the fire of Hell, and his side, his forehead and his back will be branded with them, every time they cool they will be returned to him, on a day whose length is fifty thousand years, until judgment is passed among the servants, and he sees his path, either to Paradise or to the Fire." This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih, and it is explicit that the right (haqq) on gold is obligatory just as on silver. All the scholars have agreed on this. Thus the aforementioned hadith is an explanation (bayan) of something established with certainty. It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence that an explanation may be by something weaker than what it explains, in terms of its indication and its chain, as we clarified in the introduction to this book.

It follows that the nisab of gold is twenty mithqals, and whatever exceeds it is in proportion to it. The obligatory amount on it is one-fortieth (rub' al-'ushr), as with silver. Gold and silver have no waqs (the reduction of zakat on fractions below the nisab, here meaning no exemption for partial amounts), but rather whatever exceeds the nisab is in proportion to it, contrary to whoever deviated and disagreed on some of this. And Allah knows best.

Note: the weight for the nisab of silver and gold must be taken by the weight that was known among the people of Makkah, just as the measure for the five awsuq (the nisab of grains and fruits) must be taken by the measure that was known among the people of Madina.

Al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan, in the Book of Zakat: Ahmad ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Hanzala, from Tawus, from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The measure is the measure of the people of Madina, and the weight is the weight of the people of Makkah."

Abu Dawud said in his Sunan, in the Book of Sales: Uthman ibn Abi Shayba narrated to us, Ibn Dukayn narrated to us, from Hanzala, from Tawus, from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The weight is the weight of the people of Makkah, and the measure is the measure of the people of Madina."

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: as for the hadith "The scale is the scale of the people of Makkah" to the end, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated it with chains that are sound according to the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from the narration of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. End of quote.

Abu Dawud said: it was narrated also from the narration of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. End of quote.

(p-125) Al-Khattabi said: the meaning of this hadith is that the weight upon which the right of zakat depends is the weight of the people of Makkah, which is the abode of Islam. Ibn Hazm said: I searched for it with the utmost diligence from everyone whose discernment I trusted, and all of them agreed with me that the dinar of gold in Makkah weighs eighty-two grains of unhulled barley, plus three-tenths of a grain, and the dirham is seven-tenths of the mithqal. So the weight of the dirham is fifty-seven and six-tenths of a grain, plus one-tenth of a tenth of a grain. Thus the ritl (pound) is one hundred and twenty-eight dirhams by the aforementioned dirham. End of quote.

In al-Qamus, under the root "m k k": the mithqal is one dirham and three-sevenths; the dirham is six daniq; the daniq is two qirat; the qirat is two tassuj; the tassuj is two grains; and the grain is one-sixth of one-eighth of a dirham, which is one part out of forty-eight parts of the dirham. End of quote.

We have already discussed the measure of the five awsuq in Surah al-An'am.

* *

The second issue: Are gold and silver combined with each other for zakat or not? I have not found an explicit text from the Prophet ﷺ on this, and the scholars differ about it. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, withheld judgment on combining one with the other in the narration of al-Athram and a group; and in the narration of Hanbal he decided that there is no zakat on either until each of them reaches the nisab.

Among those who said that gold and silver are not combined with each other: al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Hasan ibn Salih and Shurayk. Ibn Qudama said in al-Mughni: this was chosen by Abu Bakr Abd al-Aziz.

Among those who said that gold and silver are combined with each other to complete the nisab: Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions.

The author, may Allah forgive him, says: What appears to me to be the stronger of the two views by evidence is that gold and silver are not combined with each other, because of what is established in some sound narrations, as Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Jabir that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no zakat on what is less than five awqiya of silver," the hadith.

So if he has four ounces of silver (al-warq, which is silver), and what completes the nisab of gold, it is understood by the direct indication (dalalat al-mutabaqa) that he does not have five ounces of silver.

The Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated in this authentic hadith that there is no charity (zakat) on less than five ounces (p-126) of silver. The apparent wording of the hadith, by naming silver (al-warq), indicates that there is no zakat on less than five ounces of silver, even if one has a great deal of gold. There is no evidence from the texts that turns away from this apparent meaning. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

The third issue: Scholars differed regarding the zakat on permissible ornaments (al-huli al-mubah). A group of scholars held that there is no zakat on them. Among those who said so are Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad in the more correct of his two opinions. This was also the view of Abdullah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, Jabir ibn Abdullah, Anas ibn Malik, A'isha, and Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them all, and of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Muhammad ibn Ali, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Ibn Sirin, al-Zuhri, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Abu Ubayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir.

Among those who said that zakat is obligatory on permissible ornaments are Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mas'ud said the same, as did Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, Maymun ibn Mihran, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Sufyan al-Thawri, and Dawud. Ibn al-Mundhir also related this view from Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Ata', Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, Abdullah ibn Shaddad, and al-Zuhri.

We will mention, Allah willing, the proofs of both sides and the discussion of their evidences according to the known methods in the principles of jurisprudence and the science of hadith, so that the seeker may discern the stronger of the two opinions.

Know that whoever holds that permissible ornaments carry no zakat rests his argument on four matters:

First: a hadith reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) to this effect.

Second: authentic reports from some of the Companions, which strengthen the aforementioned hadith.

Third: analogy (qiyas).

Fourth: the lexical meaning of the language (wad' al-lugha).

As for the hadith: it is what al-Bayhaqi reported in Ma'rifat al-Sunan wa'l-Athar through the chain of Afiya ibn Ayyub, from al-Layth, from Abu'l-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "There is no zakat on ornaments."

Al-Bayhaqi said: This hadith has no basis. It is only reported from Jabir as his own statement, not as a marfu' (attributed to the Prophet) report. And what is reported from Afiya ibn Ayyub, from al-Layth, from Abu'l-Zubayr, from Jabir as marfu' has no basis. Afiya ibn Ayyub is unknown (majhul). Whoever argues with it as marfu' is risking his religion and falls into what we criticize the opponents for, arguing with the reports of liars. May Allah protect us from the likes of this.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: What al-Hafiz al-Bayhaqi, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said, that ruling by the report of Afiya mentioned for this hadith as marfu' is of the kind of arguing with the reports of liars, is open to question. This is because no one has said that Afiya is a liar. At most, al-Bayhaqi thought he was unknown, since he did not know of his reliability, whereas others knew that he was reliable and declared him reliable. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted his authentication from Abu Zur'a. Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis: "Afiya ibn Ayyub, it was said: weak." Ibn al-Jawzi said: "We know of no criticism of him." Al-Bayhaqi said: "Unknown." But Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted his authentication from Abu Zur'a.

It is not hidden that whoever says he is unknown is outweighed by whoever says he is reliable, because the latter knows what the former did not know, and whoever memorized is a proof over whoever did not memorize. Criticism is not accepted when it is vague, and one witness suffices for both authentication and criticism in narration (though not in testimony), according to the correct view. Al-Iraqi said in his Alfiyya:

"They deemed sufficient a single witness, in criticism and in authentication, unlike testimony in court."
"Authentication is accepted in general terms, but criticism is not, due to the disagreement over its causes."

Al-Iraqi said in his Alfiyya:

"They approved the acceptance of authentication without mention of its grounds, if they were heavy."
"They did not accept vague criticism, due to disagreement over its causes, and it is often clarified."
"Criticism that does not harm, as Shu'ba explained it by 'running' (rakd), is what the custodians of narrations hold, like the two shaykhs of the Sahih along with the people of reasoning, etc."

This is the correct view. There is no doubt that al-Bayhaqi's statement that Afiya is unknown is outweighed by Abu Zur'a's statement that he is reliable, because whoever memorized is a proof over whoever did not memorize. And once reliance on the aforementioned hadith is established, it is explicit on the point under dispute.

What supports the authentication of Afiya mentioned is that Ibn al-Jawzi, despite his wide knowledge and intense investigation of the narrators, said that he knows of no criticism of him.

As for the reports indicating this: among them is what Imam Malik reported in al-Muwatta', from (p-128) Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father: "A'isha, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), used to take care of her orphaned nieces under her guardianship, who had ornaments, and she did not pay zakat from their ornaments." This chain from A'isha is, as you see, of the highest authenticity.

Among them is also what Malik reported in al-Muwatta', from Nafi', from Abdullah ibn Umar: that he would adorn his daughters and slave-girls with gold, and then did not pay zakat from their ornaments. This chain from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is, as you see, of the highest authenticity.

As for what some scholars said, that the reason for not paying zakat in the first case was that it was an orphan girl's property and that a child is not obligated to pay zakat just as he is not obligated to pray, this is rejected, since A'isha held that zakat is obligatory on orphans' property. Thus the reason for not paying her zakat was that it was permissible ornament, according to the verification, not that it was an orphan's property. Likewise, the claim that the reason Ibn Umar did not pay zakat on ornaments was that they belonged to slave-girls, and that a slave owes no zakat, is also rejected, since he did not pay zakat on his daughters' ornaments, even though he married off a daughter for a thousand dinars and adorned her with four hundred of them, and did not pay zakat on that ornament. His abandoning its zakat was because it was permissible ornament, according to the verification.

Among the reports on this is what al-Shafi'i reported: Sufyan informed us, from Amr ibn Dinar: I heard a man asking Jabir ibn Abdullah about ornaments, and he said: "Its zakat is its lending (ariyya)." Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it in al-Sunan al-Kubra, and Ibn Hajar in al-Talkhis. Al-Bayhaqi added: "Even if it reaches a thousand dinars." Jabir said: "That is a great deal."

Among them is what al-Bayhaqi reported from Ali ibn Sulaym, who said: I asked Anas ibn Malik about ornaments, and he said: "There is no zakat on them."

Among them is what al-Bayhaqi reported from Asma' bint Abi Bakr: that she used to adorn her daughters with gold and did not pay zakat on it, about fifty thousand.

As for analogy (qiyas), it is of two aspects:

First: since ornaments are for mere use and not for trade and growth, they are attached to other precious stones such as pearls and coral, on the common ground that each is prepared for use and not for growth. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to this attachment in al-Muwatta' by saying: "As for raw gold and broken ornaments which their owners want to repair and wear, they are like goods kept by their people, so there is no zakat on them for their owners." Malik said: "There is no zakat on pearls, musk, or ambergris."

The second aspect of analogy is the type known as qiyas al-aks (reverse analogy), which he indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud in his words in the book on argumentation (al-istidlal):

"From it is the analogy of logic and its converse, and from it the absence of a condition, without confusion."

Some scholars disagreed about accepting this type of analogy. Its definition: it is establishing the reverse of the ruling of one thing for another, because the two are reversed in their cause. An example is the hadith of Muslim: "Does one of us fulfill his desire and have a reward for it?" He said: "Tell me, if he had placed it in something forbidden, would he bear a burden for it?" In this hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) established a reward for lawful intercourse, which is the reverse of the ruling for unlawful intercourse, which carries a burden, because the two are reversed in their cause: the cause of the reward in the first is preserving his wife and himself, and the cause of the burden in the second is that it is fornication.

Among the examples of this type of analogy according to the Malikis is their argument that ablution is not obligatory due to a large amount of vomit, because since it is not obligatory for a small amount, it is not obligatory for a large amount, the reverse of urine, since when it is obligatory for a small amount it is obligatory for a large amount.

Among its examples according to the Hanafis is their saying: since retaliation (qisas) is not obligated for a small blow with a blunt weapon, it is not obligated for a large one, the reverse of a sharp weapon, since when it is obligated for a small one it is obligated for a large one.

The way this type of analogy applies to the question we are discussing is this: goods are not subject to zakat in their own substance, but when they are for trade and growth, zakat becomes obligatory on them, the reverse of the substance (ayn), since zakat is obligatory on the substance itself. So when it is made into permissible ornament for use, and the intention of growth through trade is cut off from it, there is no zakat on it. Thus their rulings are reversed, because the two are reversed in their cause. Some Shafi'is prohibited this type of analogy, and Ibn Muhriz said it is weaker than analogy of resemblance (qiyas al-shabah). But it is not hidden that analogy is reinforced by the aforementioned marfu' hadith and the established reports from some Companions, because it is established in the principles that agreement of the text with analogy is among the factors of preference.

As for the lexical meaning, some scholars say: the words used in the sahih reports about zakat on the substance do not include ornaments in the language of the Arabs.

Abu Ubayd said: "The riqqa (silver) among the Arabs is minted silver with the stamp circulating among people, and the Arabs do not apply it to worked metal. The same was said regarding the ounce (uqiyya)."

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: What Abu Ubayd said is the known usage in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Jawhari said in his Sihah: "Al-warq: minted dirhams, and likewise al-riqqa, and the ha' is a substitute for the waw." In al-Qamus: "Al-warq, with three vowel forms, and like kataf: minted dirhams, its plural awraq and wiraq, like riqqa."

This is the substance of the argument of those who say there is no zakat on ornaments.

As for what some scholars claimed, arguing for this from the practice of the people of Madina, it is objected that some people of Madina disagree on this. The argument from the practice of the people of Madina, according to those who hold it, Malik, is only where they agree on a matter where opinion has no room, not where they disagree, or where it is among the matters of ijtihad, as he indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud in his words:

"And they made the Madinan practice authoritative in what is founded on revelation (tawqif), while it was said: absolutely..."

Because by "Madinan" he means the Madinan consensus that occurred among the Companions or the Successors, not what they disagreed on, as in this question. He restricted it to what is founded on revelation, not matters of ijtihad, according to the correct view.

As for the argument of those who hold that zakat is obligatory on ornaments: it is also confined to four matters:

First: hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he made zakat obligatory on ornaments.

Second: reports transmitted to this effect from some Companions.

Third: lexical meaning.

Fourth: analogy.

The traditions on this matter include what Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan*: Abu Kamil and Humayd ibn Mas'adah (the wording is close) narrated to us that Khalid ibn al-Harith told them: Husayn narrated to us, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that a woman came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and with her was her daughter, and on her daughter's wrist were two thick gold bracelets. He said to her: "Do you pay the zakat on this?" She said: "No." He said: "Would it please you that Allah adorn you with two bracelets of fire on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: she took them off and threw them to the Prophet (ﷺ), and said: "They are for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and for His Messenger."

al-Nasa'i said in his *Sunan*: Isma'il ibn Mas'ud informed us, he said: Khalid narrated to us, from Husayn, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: "That a woman from the people of Yemen came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and with her was a daughter of hers, and on her daughter's wrist were two thick gold bracelets. He said: 'Do you pay the zakat on this?' She said: 'No.' He said: 'Would it please you that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, adorn you with two bracelets of fire on the Day of Resurrection?' He said: she took them off and threw them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said: 'They are for Allah and for His Messenger (ﷺ).'"

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la informed us, he said: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, he said: I heard Husayn say: Amr ibn Shu'ayb narrated to me, he said: "A woman came, and with her was her daughter, and on her daughter's wrists were two bracelets," similar to it. It is *mursal* (its chain omits a companion). Abu Abd al-Rahman (al-Nasa'i) said: Khalid is more reliable (*athbat*) than al-Mu'tamir. End of quotation.

This hadith, which Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i reported through the chain of Husayn al-Mu'allim from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, is at its lowest level *hasan* (good). By this you know that the statement of al-Tirmidhi, may Allah have mercy on him, that "nothing sound (*sahih*) is related on this subject," is not correct, because he was unaware of Husayn al-Mu'allim's narration of it from Amr ibn Shu'ayb. Rather, he firmly stated that it was not narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb except through Ibn Lahi'ah and al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabbah, and that Hajjaj ibn Artah followed them, and all of them are weak.

Among them is what Abu Dawud also related: Muhammad ibn Isa narrated to us, Attab, meaning Ibn Bashir, narrated to us, from Thabit ibn Ajlan, from Ata', "from Umm Salamah, she said: I used to wear gold ornaments, so I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it a treasure (*kanz*)?' He said: 'What reaches the point that its zakat is paid, and its zakat is paid, is not a treasure.'" al-Hakim, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi also reported something similar. End of quotation.

Among them is also what Abu Dawud related: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Razi narrated to us, Amr ibn al-Rabi' ibn Tariq narrated to us, Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated to us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far, that Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata' informed him, from Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Had, that he said: "We entered upon Aisha, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), and she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me and saw in my hands rings (*fatakhat*) of silver. He said: 'What is this, O Aisha?' I said: 'I made them so that I may adorn myself for you, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Do you pay their zakat?' I said: 'No,' or 'what Allah willed.' He said: 'It is enough for you of the Fire.'"

Safwan ibn Salih narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Umar ibn Ya'la, and he mentioned the hadith similar to the hadith of the ring. It was said to Sufyan: "How does one pay its zakat?" He said: "You add it to something else." End of quotation.

This hadith of Aisha, al-Hakim, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi also reported something similar to it. End of quotation.

al-Daraqutni reported from Aisha, through the chain of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from Urwah, from her, that she said: "There is no harm in wearing jewelry if its zakat is given." End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb has been supported by the hadith of Umm Salamah and the hadith of Aisha, and he cited them.

Among them is what Imam Ahmad related from Asma' bint Yazid, with the wording: she said: "I and my maternal aunt entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and we were wearing gold bracelets. He said to us: 'Do you give their zakat?' We said: 'No.' He said: 'Are you not afraid that Allah will adorn you with a bracelet of fire? Pay its zakat.'" End of quotation.

al-Daraqutni related something similar from the hadith of Fatimah bint Qays, and in its chain is Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, who is *matruk* (abandoned). Ibn Hajar said this in *al-Talkhis*.

As for the reports from the companions: among them is what Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi related through the chain of Shu'ayb ibn Yasar, who said: "Umar wrote to Abu Musa: Command the Muslim women under your authority to give charity from their jewelry." End of quotation.

al-Bayhaqi said: This is *mursal*; Shu'ayb ibn Yasar did not meet Umar. Ibn Hajar said in *al-Talkhis*: It is *mursal*, as al-Bukhari said. al-Hasan denied this, in what Ibn Abi Shaybah related, saying: "We do not know of any of the caliphs who said: 'There is zakat on jewelry.'"

Among them is what al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Mas'ud: that his wife asked him about some jewelry she had, and he said: "When it reaches two hundred dirhams, zakat is due on it." She said: "Shall I place it with my nephews (sons of my brother) who are in my care?" He said: "Yes."

al-Bayhaqi said: This has been related as a *marfu'* (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) report, but it is nothing. He said: al-Bukhari said: it is *mursal*. al-Daraqutni related it from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud as *marfu'*, and said: This is an error; the correct version is *mawquf* (stopping at Ibn Mas'ud). Ibn Hajar said this in *al-Talkhis*.

Among them is what al-Bayhaqi related from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: that he used to write to his treasurer Salim, that he should pay the zakat on the jewelry of his daughters every year. As for what is related on this from Ibn Abbas, al-Shafi'i said: "I do not know whether it is established from him or not." Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi related it from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and others. Ibn Hajar also said this in *al-Talkhis*.

As for analogy (*qiyas*): they analogized jewelry to minted and cast (coinage) money, by the common cause that all of them are currency (*naqd*).

As for linguistic usage (*wad' al-lughah*): they claimed that the word *riqqah* (silver), and the word *uqiyyah* (ounce) established in the authentic reports, includes wrought silver just as it includes minted coinage. We have already stated that the verified position is otherwise.

Now that you know the arguments of both sides, we will mention what each of them may rely upon.

As for the view that the zakat on jewelry is obligatory, it has preferred points:

Among them: those who related it from the companions from the Prophet (ﷺ) are more numerous, as we have already mentioned their reports from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, Aisha, Umm Salamah and Asma' bint Yazid, may Allah be pleased with them all.

As for the view that zakat is not obligatory on it, it is not related as *marfu'* except through the hadith of Jabir, as has preceded.

The large number of narrators is among the preferred factors according to the verified position, as we mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah in the discussion of the verse on usury.

Among them: that its hadiths, like the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb and those mentioned with it, are stronger in chain than the hadith of the removal of zakat which was related by Afiyah ibn Ayyub.

Among them: that what indicates obligation takes precedence over what indicates permissibility, for caution in discharging the duty of the obligation, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence. To this points the statement of the author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* in the section on preference by the indication of the meaning: [Rajaz meter]
"And the one that transfers, and the one that affirms, and the one that commands after prohibitions, then this last one
Is upon permissibility..." etc.

The meaning of his statement: "then this last one is upon permissibility" is that what indicates a command takes precedence over what indicates permissibility, as we have mentioned.

Among them: the clear texts that indicate the obligation of zakat on the basic silver and gold; and this is evidence that jewelry is of the type on which zakat is obligatory in its essence. This is the summary of what can be preferred for this view.

As for the view that zakat is not obligatory on permissible jewelry, it is preferred on the basis that the hadiths that came regarding prohibition were only in the time when adorning oneself with gold was forbidden to women, and forbidden jewelry is subject to zakat by consensus.

As for the evidence for the absence of zakat on it, that is after adorning oneself with gold became permissible.

The verified position: adorning oneself with gold was at first forbidden to women, then it was permitted, as is indicated by what al-Bayhaqi cited of the evidences for its first prohibition and its later permission. By this, the evidences are reconciled (*al-jam'*), and reconciliation is obligatory if it is possible, as is established in the principles and the sciences of hadith. To this points the statement of the author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud*: [Rajaz meter]
"Reconciliation is obligatory whenever it is possible; otherwise, for the later one there is a clear abrogation (*naskh*)."

Its reasoning is evident, because acting upon both evidences is better than nullifying one of them, and it is known that reconciliation, when possible, takes precedence over all the preferential factors.

If it is said: this reconciliation is undermined by the hadith of Aisha mentioned earlier, for in it is: "He saw in my hand rings of silver," the hadith.

And *al-warq* means silver, and silver had not previously been subject to prohibition, so adorning oneself with it was never forbidden at any time.

The answer is what al-Hafiz al-Bayhaqi, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said. He said: Whoever says there is no zakat on jewelry supposes that the hadiths and reports that came regarding the obligation of its zakat were from the time when adorning oneself with gold was forbidden to women; so when it was permitted for them, its zakat was dropped.

He said: And how can this statement be correct along with the hadith of Aisha, if the mention of *al-warq* in it is preserved? However, the narration of al-Qasim and Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Aisha, regarding her leaving the payment of zakat on jewelry, along with what is established of her view on paying zakat on the wealth of orphans, casts doubt upon this attributed report. For she does not oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) in what she related from him, except in what she knew to be abrogated. End of quotation.

We have already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah the discussion of a companion's opposition to what was related regarding the verse of divorce. In sum, it is not hidden that it is unlikely that Aisha would know that the non-payment of zakat on jewelry incurs the threat from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is enough for her of the Fire, and then she would leave off paying it after that on behalf of those in her care, while she is known for her view on the obligation of zakat on the wealth of orphans.

Among the answers of the people of this view: that what is meant by the zakat on jewelry is its lending (*ariyah*). This was related by al-Bayhaqi from Ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and al-Sha'bi, in one of the two reports from him.

This is the summary of the discussion on this question.

The strongest of the approaches according to what is established in the principles and the science of hadith is reconciliation when it is possible, and it is possible here.

The author of these notes, may Allah forgive him, says: Paying the zakat on jewelry is more cautious, because "Whoever avoids doubtful matters has cleared himself regarding his religion and his honor," and "Leave what makes you doubtful for what does not make you doubtful." And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

Fourth issue: Know that the majority of the scholars of the Muslims, from the companions and those after them, hold that zakat is obligatory on trade goods (*urud al-tijarah*). They are valued at the end of the year, and one-fortieth (a quarter of a tenth) of their value is paid, like the zakat on currency. Ibn al-Mundhir said: The majority of the people of knowledge agreed on the obligation of zakat on trade. He said: We have related it from Umar ibn al-Khattab, his son Abd Allah, Ibn Abbas, and the seven jurists: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith, Kharijah ibn Zayd, Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah, and Sulayman ibn Yasar; also al-Hasan al-Basri, Tawus, Jabir ibn Zayd, Maymun ibn Mihran, al-Nakha'i, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, al-Nu'man and his companions, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and Abu Ubayd. End of quotation, as conveyed by al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, and Ibn Qudamah in *al-Mughni*.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, has a distinction regarding trade goods, because trade goods in his view are divided into the goods of an active trader (*mudir*) and the goods of a hoarding trader (*muhtakir*). The active trader is one who buys and sells constantly; the hoarder is one who buys goods and waits for them until their price rises and then sells them; and if their price does not rise, he does not sell them even if they remain for years.

So for the active trader, his goods and his debts which he is claiming from people, if they are expected to be recovered, he pays zakat on them at the end of each year; a debt that is due (*hal*) he pays zakat on by its count (*bi-l-'adad*), and a deferred debt (*mu'ajjal*) by its value (*bi-l-qimah*).

Regarding the goods of the hoarder (al-muhtakir): they are not valued in his possession, and there is no zakat on them until they are sold for cash, whereupon he pays zakat on the cash for one lunar year counted from the start of the year of the original goods. Ibn 'Ashir alluded to this in *al-Murshid al-Mu'in* with his words, in rajaz meter:

> The goods of trade and the debt of one who has them in circulation,
> their value is like cash, and then one who hoards them.
>
> He pays zakat on the receipt of a price or a debt, in cash, on condition of the year for both origins.

Malik added, in the well-known position of his school, a condition: for the zakat on the goods of the one who runs a trade (al-mudir) to be obligatory, some cash of gold or silver must come into his hand, even if it is a quarter dirham or less. Ibn Habib, from among the people of his school, disagreed with him and agreed with the majority in not requiring this.

It is not hidden that the position of the majority is the apparent one. We do not know of anyone among the scholars who disagreed about the obligation of zakat on trade goods, except what is reported from Dawud al-Zahiri and some of his followers.

The majority's evidence consists of a verse, hadiths, and reports transmitted from some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It is not known that any of them disagreed about this, so it is a silent consensus (ijma' sukuti).

Among the hadiths indicating this is what Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "For camels there is their zakat, for sheep there is their zakat, and for cloth (al-bazz) there is its zakat," the hadith in full. It was recorded by al-Hakim, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi.

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: "This hadith was narrated by al-Daraqutni in his *Sunan*, by al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah in his *al-Mustadrak*, and by al-Bayhaqi, with their chains of transmission. Al-Hakim cited it with two chains and then said: these two chains are sound according to the condition of al-Bukhari and Muslim." End of quote.

He then said: the phrase "and for cloth there is its zakat" is with a fatha on the ba' and with a zay. This is how all the narrators transmitted it, and al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi explicitly stated the zay. Ibn Hajar said in *al-Talkhis*: the hadith of Abu Dharr, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "For camels there is their zakat and for cloth there is its zakat," was recorded by al-Daraqutni from Abu Dharr by two routes, and at its end is "and for cloth there is its zakat," said with a zay, and its chain is not sound; it revolves around Musa ibn 'Ubayda al-Rabadhi. He has a third route in al-Daraqutni, through Ibn Jurayj, from 'Imran ibn Abi Anas, from Malik ibn Aws, from Abu Dharr, and it is defective (ma'lul), because Ibn Jurayj narrated from 'Imran that it reached him from him. al-Tirmidhi recorded it in *al-'Ilal* by this route and said: I asked al-Bukhari about it and he said: Ibn Jurayj did not hear it from 'Imran. It has a fourth route, also recorded by al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim, through Sa'id ibn Salama ibn Abi al-Husam, from 'Imran, and its wording is: "For camels there is their zakat, for sheep there is their zakat, for cattle there is their zakat, and for cloth there is its zakat, and whoever hoards dirhams or dinars, not preparing them for a creditor and not spending them in the way of Allah, then it is a treasure with which he will be branded on the Day of Resurrection." This is a chain with no harm in it (la ba'sa bihi). End of quote.

So you see that Ibn Hajar said this chain is "no harm in it," together with what we have already cited from al-Hakim about the soundness of the two chains mentioned, and al-Nawawi's authentication of that. However, what I have seen in the *Sunan* of al-Bayhaqi is that Sa'id ibn Salama ibn Abi al-Husam narrates the hadith from the aforementioned Musa, from 'Imran, not from 'Imran directly. So look into it.

If it is said: Ibn Daqiq al-'Id said: What I have seen in a copy of *al-Mustadrak* in this hadith is "al-burr" (wheat), with a damma on the ba' and with the unpointed ra'. The narration of al-Daraqutni in which he explicitly stated the zay in the word "al-bazz" in the hadith is weak. Therefore there is no evidence in the hadith for establishing its soundness as proof of the obligation of zakat on trade goods.
